items.new: We were weaving and weaving away like this when a sound made me start — a sound so strange, so drawn-out, so musically wild and unearthly, that the ball of free will fell from my hand, and I stood staring up at the clouds that voice had dropped from like a wing. High up in the crosstrees was that mad Gay Header, Tashtego. He was leaning eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and in brief, sudden bursts he kept up his cries. Of course, that same sound was perhaps ringing out at that very moment all over the seas, from hundreds of whalemen's lookouts perched just as high; but few of those lungs could have given that familiar old cry such a marvelous cadence as Tashtego the Indian's did.

items.new: There is one more small point about gamming that must not be forgotten here. Every profession has its own little peculiarities of detail, and so does the whale fishery. On a pirate ship, a man-of-war, or a slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern sheets on a comfortable seat, sometimes a cushioned one, and often does his own steering with a pretty little milliner's tiller trimmed with gay cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no seat in the stern, no sofa of any kind, and no tiller at all. It would be high times indeed if whaling captains were wheeled over the water on casters, like gouty old aldermen in patent chairs. As for a tiller, the whale-boat never stands for any such effeminacy. So, since a whole boat's crew must leave the ship when gamming, and since the boat-steerer, or harpooner, is one of them, that subordinate does the steering on these occasions, and the captain, with nowhere to sit, is rowed off to his visit standing straight up like a pine tree. You will often notice that this standing captain, aware that the eyes of the whole visible world are fixed on him from the sides of both ships, is keenly conscious of how important it is to keep his dignity by keeping his feet. That is no easy matter. Behind him the huge projecting steering oar knocks him now and then in the small of the back, and in front the after-oar returns the compliment by rapping his knees. So he is wedged in completely, front and back, and can only widen himself sideways by settling down on his spread legs; but a sudden, violent pitch of the boat will often come close to toppling him, because a long foundation is worthless without a matching breadth. Just set two poles in a spread angle, and you will not be able to stand them up. Then again, it would never do — never, I say — for this straddling captain to be seen, in plain view of the world's riveted eyes, steadying himself the least bit by grabbing anything with his hands. In fact, to show his complete, buoyant self-command, he usually keeps his hands in his trouser pockets; though perhaps, since they are usually very large, heavy hands, he keeps them there as ballast. Still, there have been cases, and well-documented ones too, where a captain has been known, for an unusually critical moment or two — in a sudden squall, say — to grab the nearest oarsman's hair and hang on like grim death.

Source says the dolphin 'was drawn' on temple panels, pedestals, shields, medallions, cups and coins; 'carved' narrows the medium, which does not fit painted cups or struck coins. Use a neutral verb.
items.new: The first source of all these pictorial delusions may lie among the oldest Hindu, Egyptian, and Greek sculptures. Ever since those inventive but unscrupulous ages, when the dolphin was portrayed on the marble panels of temples, on the pedestals of statues, and on shields, medallions, cups, and coins, wearing scales of chain-mail like Saladin's and a helmeted head like St. George's — ever since then, the same sort of license has held sway, not only in most popular pictures of the whale but in many scientific depictions of him too.

items.new: True, landsmen in general have always looked on the native inhabitants of the seas with feelings unspeakably unsociable and repellent. We know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so much so that Columbus sailed over countless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one. By far the most terrible of all mortal disasters have, since time immemorial, struck down tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone to sea, without distinction. And a moment's thought will show that however much baby man may boast of his science and skill, and however much that science and skill may grow in a flattering future, the sea will go on insulting and murdering him forever and ever, to the crack of doom, and pulverizing the stateliest, stiffest frigate he can build. Yet for all that, the constant repetition of these very impressions has made man lose the sense of the sea's full awfulness that originally belongs to it.
